Figure 7. Log-probability of Ipsos’s result as a function of the assumed effective sample size. Every line is far below the conventional 5% and 1-in-a-million thresholds at every n.

8.3 Varying the population: excluding Kosovo i Metohija and the diaspora

Ipsos surveyed only citizens present in Serbia without Kosovo i Metohija. Voters abroad broke overwhelmingly for Studentska lista (72.8% of their valid votes), voters in Kosovo i Metohija overwhelmingly for Ujedinjena Srbija (73.8%). The fair comparison removes both from the population.

scheme_a_adj <- scheme_a |>
  dplyr::mutate(votes_adj = votes - kim - abroad,
                rik_p_adj = votes_adj / sum(votes_adj),
                rik_pct_adj = 100 * rik_p_adj)
p_rik_A_adj <- setNames(scheme_a_adj$rik_p_adj, scheme_a_adj$group)
g_adj  <- g_test(k_ips_A, p_rik_A_adj)
bin_adj <- c(binom_tail(k_ips_A[1], n_primary, p_rik_A_adj[1], "low"),
             binom_tail(k_ips_A[2], n_primary, p_rik_A_adj[2], "high"))

scheme_a_adj |>
  dplyr::transmute(Category = group, `RIK % (all voters)` = fmt_pct(rik_pct),
                   `RIK % (Serbia proper, without Kosovo i Metohija and abroad)` = fmt_pct(rik_pct_adj),
                   `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(ipsos_pct, 1)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 13. The population redefined to match Ipsos's sampling frame (removes %s ballots).",
                                 fmt_n(sum(scheme_a$kim + scheme_a$abroad))))
Table 13. The population redefined to match Ipsos’s sampling frame (removes 115,241 ballots).
Category RIK % (all voters) RIK % (Serbia proper, without Kosovo i Metohija and abroad) Ipsos %
Studentska lista 53.03% 52.94% 40.0%
Ujedinjena Srbija 38.97% 38.96% 47.4%
Manjinske liste 2.16% 2.21% 2.3%
Other 5.84% 5.89% 10.3%

Result. Matching Ipsos’s sampling frame moves the Studentska lista share from 53.03% to 52.94% and Ujedinjena Srbija from 38.97% to 38.96%: changes in the second decimal, because the two excluded populations are small and pull in opposite directions. The G-test probability rises slightly, from 3 × 10−36 (about 1 in a 3 followed by 35 zeros) to 1 × 10−35 (about 1 in a 9 followed by 34 zeros). The population definition is not the explanation.

8.4 Varying the base: valid votes only

As explained in Section 4 (Issue 1), Ipsos’s 2.5% invalid share is an assumption rather than a measurement, so it should not really be allowed to count as “sampling evidence”. Here we remove invalid ballots from both sides: Ipsos’s list shares are rescaled to the 97.5% that its respondents actually produced, and RIK’s shares are taken over valid votes. This is the fairest version of the test for Ipsos.

# Scheme A on the valid-vote base: drop the invalid row from both sources
ips_valid <- ipsos |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::group_by(group) |> dplyr::summarise(pct = sum(ipsos_pct) / 0.975, .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = grp_levels)) |> dplyr::arrange(group)
rik_valid <- rik |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::group_by(group) |> dplyr::summarise(votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = grp_levels)) |> dplyr::arrange(group)
p_rik_A_valid   <- setNames(rik_valid$votes / sum(rik_valid$votes), grp_levels)
pct_ips_A_valid <- setNames(ips_valid$pct, grp_levels)
k_ips_A_valid   <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A_valid, n_primary, 4)
g_valid   <- g_test(k_ips_A_valid, p_rik_A_valid)
bin_valid <- binom_tail(k_ips_A_valid[1], n_primary, p_rik_A_valid[1], "low")

# Scheme B on the valid-vote base
sb_valid <- scheme_b |> dplyr::filter(short != "Invalid ballots") |>
  dplyr::mutate(p = votes / sum(votes), pct = ipsos_pct / 0.975)
k_B_valid <- pct_to_counts(sb_valid$pct, n_primary, which.max(sb_valid$pct)); names(k_B_valid) <- sb_valid$short
p_B_valid <- setNames(sb_valid$p, sb_valid$short)
small_v   <- n_primary * p_B_valid < 5
k_B_valid2 <- c(k_B_valid[!small_v], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(k_B_valid[small_v]))
p_B_valid2 <- c(p_B_valid[!small_v], `Small lists (merged)` = sum(p_B_valid[small_v]))
gB_valid <- g_test(k_B_valid2, p_B_valid2)

tibble::tibble(
  Test = c("Studentska lista this low or lower (binomial)", "G test, Scheme A", "G test, Scheme B"),
  `All ballots (main analysis)` = purrr::map_chr(c(m2$log10_p[1], gA["log10_p_G"], gB["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p),
  `Valid votes only` = purrr::map_chr(c(bin_valid, g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"]), fmt_log10p)
) |> kable_report(caption = "Table 14. The key tests with invalid ballots removed from both sources.")
Table 14. The key tests with invalid ballots removed from both sources.
Test All ballots (main analysis) Valid votes only
Studentska lista this low or lower (binomial) 2 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 4 followed by 32 zeros) 1 × 10−31 (about 1 in a 8 followed by 30 zeros)
G test, Scheme A 3 × 10−36 (about 1 in a 3 followed by 35 zeros) 8 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 1 followed by 32 zeros)
G test, Scheme B 1 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 9 followed by 32 zeros) 1 × 10−30 (about 1 in a 7 followed by 29 zeros) 
# the overall range of tail probabilities across methods AND bases, used in the conclusions
tail_range_all <- range(c(tail_range, g_valid["log10_p_G"], gB_valid["log10_p_G"]))

Result. On the valid-vote base Studentska lista’s true share is 53.72% and Ipsos’s rescaled estimate 41.0%; the gap narrows by a fraction of a point and the “Other” category loses the 1.2-point invalid-ballot overestimate. The probabilities move accordingly: the Scheme A test from 10−35 to 10−32, Scheme B from 10−33 to 10−30. Three or four powers of ten is a real difference, and it is the reason this document reports its headline as an order of magnitude rather than a precise figure. It does not come close to changing the conclusion.

Across every combination of sample size, population definition and base, the probability of Ipsos’s result under random sampling never rises above about 10−25. The conclusion of Section 7 is not an artefact of our choices.

9 What would it take to rescue the poll?

9.1 Why ask

A probability of 10−36 is not a number anyone can feel. A more useful way to express the same finding is to ask: how large would each innocent explanation have to be to make Ipsos’s result ordinary? This section quantifies the three explanations that concern the electorate rather than the pollster’s instrument: a genuine late swing of opinion, differential turnout, and the behaviour of undecided voters.

9.2 Scenario 1: a late swing between 22 and 25 October

Suppose the electorate on 22 October was closer to Ipsos’s picture than the final result shows, and that voters then moved in the final three days. How many would have had to move for Ipsos’s result to have been merely unlucky, i.e. to have had a 5% probability, the conventional border of “could be chance”?

Ipsos’s picture differs from the result in all four categories (too few Studentska voters, too many Ujedinjena Srbija voters, and too many voters for the small lists and invalid ballots), so the cleanest way to pose the question is this: suppose the electorate on 22 October was somewhere on the straight line between Ipsos’s picture and the actual result, and then drifted towards the actual result by election day. How far along that line towards Ipsos’s picture would the electorate have had to be for Ipsos’s poll to have had a 5% probability? We express the answer as the number of voters who would then have had to switch to Studentska lista in the final three days. Moving along this particular line is also the direction that needs the fewest movers (any swing that left the small-list excess in place could never rescue the poll), so the figure below is a lower bound, i.e. the most generous answer for Ipsos.

p_ips_A <- pct_ips_A / 100
# population a fraction t of the way from the actual result towards Ipsos's picture
swing_log10p <- function(t, k = k_ips_A, p_from = p_rik_A, p_to = p_ips_A) {
  p2 <- (1 - t) * p_from + t * p_to
  g_test(k, p2)["log10_p_G"]
}
t_05 <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root
t_50 <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t) - log10(0.50), c(0, 1))$root
to_sl <- function(t) t * (p_rik_A[1] - p_ips_A[1]) * rik_meta$ballots       # voters who must move TO Studentska
from_us <- function(t) t * (p_ips_A[2] - p_rik_A[2]) * rik_meta$ballots     # ... of whom from Ujedinjena Srbija
voters_05 <- to_sl(t_05); voters_50 <- to_sl(t_50)

swing_df <- tibble::tibble(t = seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(voters = to_sl(t), log10_p = purrr::map_dbl(t, swing_log10p))

# how much does the answer depend on the assumed sample size?
voters_05_by_n <- vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  k <- pct_to_counts(pct_ips_A, n, 4)
  to_sl(uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t, k = k) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root)
}, numeric(1))
ggplot(swing_df, aes(x = voters, y = log10_p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(0.05), linetype = "dotted", colour = "#898781") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = log10(0.05), label = "p = 0.05 (“could be chance”)", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.6, colour = "#52514e") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = voters_05, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("label", x = voters_05, y = min(swing_df$log10_p) * 0.5,
           label = sprintf("about %s voters\nwould have had to move\nto Studentska lista", fmt_n(round(voters_05, -3))),
           hjust = 1.05, size = 3.5, colour = "#eb6834", fill = "#fcfcfb", label.size = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) parse(text = paste0("10^", x)), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = "Voters assumed to have moved to Studentska lista between 22 and 25 October",
       y = "Probability of Ipsos's result", title = "Scenario 1: how big a late swing would rescue the poll?") +
  theme_report()

Figure 8. How the probability of Ipsos’s result rises as we assume ever more voters moved to Studentska lista after the poll (the electorate drifting from Ipsos’s picture towards the actual result).

Result. For Ipsos’s result to have been merely a 1-in-20 unlucky draw, the electorate on 22 October would have had to be 78% of the way from the actual result to Ipsos’s picture, which means that about 450,000 voters (10.2% of all ballots cast) would have had to move to Studentska lista in the three days after the fieldwork, roughly 291,000 of them from Ujedinjena Srbija and the rest voters who would otherwise have backed a small list or cast an invalid ballot. (The figure depends a little on the assumed sample size: between 428,000 and 480,000 across the range of n used in Section 8.) For Ipsos’s poll to have been a typical, median poll, about 507,000 voters would have had to move. That is a swing of some 10 points within 72 hours, in an election where no event of that magnitude was reported between 22 and 25 October; it would mean Ujedinjena Srbija losing about one in 7 of its 22-October supporters by polling day. Late swings of one to three points are common in the polling literature; a swing of this size within three days is, to our knowledge, undocumented in comparable elections. (For what polling error normally looks like across 351 elections in 45 countries, see Jennings & Wlezien, 2018; for a forensic account of an unusually bad polling year and why non-response rather than late swing or turnout models was the likely cause, see the AAPOR Task Force report on 2020 U.S. pre-election polls.)

9.3 Scenario 2: differential turnout (the net surplus)

Ipsos predicted a turnout of 64.7%; actual turnout was 68.98%. The difference is about 275,000 voters who turned out but whom Ipsos’s model expected to stay home. (The two percentages have slightly different bases, Ipsos’s being adults in Serbia proper and RIK’s registered voters including Kosovo i Metohija and abroad, so this is an approximation; the scenario is deliberately extreme in any case.) Could these “unexpected” voters account for the gap? We take the extreme case for this net surplus: every single one of them voted for Studentska lista. Removing them from the count gives the electorate Ipsos thought it was measuring.

registered_processed <- rik_meta$turned_out / (rik_meta$turnout_pct / 100)       # registered voters at the processed stations
extra_voters <- (rik_meta$turnout_pct - ipsos_turnout["est"]) / 100 * registered_processed
votes_t <- scheme_a$votes
votes_t[1] <- votes_t[1] - extra_voters                      # all extra voters assumed to be Studentska voters
p_turnout <- votes_t / sum(votes_t)
g_turn <- g_test(k_ips_A, p_turnout)

tibble::tibble(Category = scheme_a$group,
               `RIK % (actual)` = fmt_pct(100 * p_rik_A),
               `% if all extra turnout were Studentska voters` = fmt_pct(100 * p_turnout),
               `Ipsos %` = fmt_pct(pct_ips_A, 1)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 15. Scenario 2: the electorate Ipsos expected, under the extreme assumption that all %s voters it did not expect voted Studentska lista.", fmt_n(round(extra_voters, -3))))
Table 15. Scenario 2: the electorate Ipsos expected, under the extreme assumption that all 275,000 voters it did not expect voted Studentska lista.
Category RIK % (actual) % if all extra turnout were Studentska voters Ipsos %
Studentska lista 53.03% 49.93% 40.0%
Ujedinjena Srbija 38.97% 41.55% 47.4%
Manjinske liste 2.16% 2.30% 2.3%
Other 5.84% 6.23% 10.3%

Result. Even in this deliberately extreme scenario, in which the entire turnout surprise consists of Studentska voters, the electorate Ipsos was trying to measure would have had Studentska lista at 49.93% and Ujedinjena Srbija at 41.55%, still a clear Studentska lead and still far from Ipsos’s 40.0 / 47.4. The probability of Ipsos’s result under this adjusted population is 3 × 10−23 (about 1 in a 3 followed by 22 zeros). The turnout surplus is not the explanation.

One caveat belongs here. Turnout can also shift a poll without changing the total: if many people who told Ipsos they would vote for Ujedinjena Srbija stayed at home, while an equal number who had said they would not vote turned out for Studentska lista, aggregate turnout is unchanged but the electorate Ipsos modelled is not the one that voted. Such gross flows are a failure of the pollster’s likely-voter model rather than of sampling, and they are not observable from the outside; to produce Ipsos’s picture they would have to involve several hundred thousand voters swapping places. We treat this, together with the handling of undecided respondents, under Scenario 4 and under non-sampling error in the conclusions.

9.4 Scenario 3: both together

Combining the two, an extreme turnout assumption and a late swing, how large would the swing still have to be?

t_05_comb <- uniroot(function(t) swing_log10p(t, p_from = p_turnout) - log10(0.05), c(0, 1))$root
voters_05_comb <- t_05_comb * (p_turnout[1] - p_ips_A[1]) * sum(votes_t)

Result. With the extreme turnout assumption already in place, a further 298,000 voters (7.2% of the remaining ballots) would still have had to move to Studentska lista in three days to bring Ipsos’s result up to a 5% probability. The two electorate-side explanations do not add up to an explanation.

9.5 Scenario 4: undecided voters

Ipsos’s percentages describe only the respondents who named a list. Section 6 suggested that this “decided” base was perhaps 78% of the sample, leaving roughly a fifth undecided. Suppose Ipsos’s decided respondents were a perfect picture of the decided electorate, and that the entire gap arose because the undecided voters, once they made up their minds, voted very differently. How lopsided would their choice have had to be?

If a share u of eventual voters was undecided at the time of the poll, the final result is (1 − u) × (Ipsos’s decided picture) + u × (how the undecided voted). Knowing the final result and Ipsos’s picture, we can solve for the third term.

undec <- purrr::map_dfr(c(0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50), function(u) {
  q <- (p_rik_A - (1 - u) * p_ips_A) / u          # how the undecided must have voted
  tibble::tibble(u = u,
                 `Studentska lista` = 100 * q[1], `Ujedinjena Srbija` = 100 * q[2],
                 `Manjinske liste` = 100 * q[3], Other = 100 * q[4])
})
undec |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Undecided share` = fmt_pct(100 * u, 0), .keep = "unused", .before = 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-`Undecided share`, ~ gsub("-", "−", sprintf("%.0f%%", .x)))) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 16. Scenario 4: how the undecided voters would have had to split for Ipsos's decided picture to have been exactly right. Negative values are impossible.")
Table 16. Scenario 4: how the undecided voters would have had to split for Ipsos’s decided picture to have been exactly right. Negative values are impossible.
Undecided share Studentska lista Ujedinjena Srbija Manjinske liste Other
20% 105% 5% 2% −12%
25% 92% 14% 2% −8%
30% 83% 19% 2% −5%
40% 73% 26% 2% −1%
50% 66% 31% 2% 1%

Result. If a fifth of the eventual voters were undecided when Ipsos polled, no split works at all: they would have had to vote more than 100% for Studentska lista. With a quarter undecided they would have had to vote 92% for Studentska lista and 14% for Ujedinjena Srbija; with a third undecided, 83% and 19%. And in every row up to about 40% undecided the small lists come out negative: because Ipsos put the small lists and invalid ballots too high as well, no split of the undecided voters can reconcile the whole vector; they would have had to take votes away from the small lists, which is impossible. Undecided voters do break unevenly in real elections, and a late-deciding bloc favouring a protest movement is entirely plausible; a bloc of this size voting almost unanimously is not what the literature describes. This scenario is also, like the previous two, the most generous reading possible: it assumes Ipsos’s decided respondents were a perfect sample, with zero sampling error of their own.

10 Summary and conclusions

10.1 What we did

  1. Collected both records. Ipsos’s final estimate of 22 October 2026 (n = 3,624; Ujedinjena Srbija 47.4%, Studentska lista 40.0%, with 95% intervals of about ±2.1 points, commissioned by the Ujedinjena Srbija list) and RIK’s count as of 31 October 2026 (8,339 of 8,392 polling stations; Studentska lista 53.03%, Ujedinjena Srbija 38.97%; turnout 68.98%).
  2. Made them comparable. Both use “all ballots cast” as the base, so no rescaling was needed. We grouped the lists into Studentska lista, Ujedinjena Srbija, the four manjinske liste that entered Parliament, and everything else. Ipsos’s error is concentrated in the two large lists, 13.0 points too low for Studentska lista and 8.4 points too high for Ujedinjena Srbija, with the remaining 4.6 points spread as small overestimates across the minor lists, the minority lists and invalid ballots.
  3. Established the effective sample size from Ipsos’s own confidence intervals: about 2,110 decided respondents, the most generous figure the published precision supports.
  4. Computed the probability of Ipsos’s result under the hypothesis that it was a random sample of the actual electorate, in five different ways, including an exact computation that enumerates every possible outcome of the poll, two simulation estimates, and the textbook chi-square approximation.
  5. Stress-tested the result against every alternative sample size, population definition and base (all ballots versus valid votes).
  6. Quantified what a late swing, a turnout surprise or a lopsided break of undecided voters would have had to look like to explain the gap.

10.2 What we found

≈ 2 × 10−36
the probability that a random sample of the people who voted on 25 October 2026 would produce a result at least as far from the truth as Ipsos’s published numbers (exact multinomial test, all 1,570,111,136 possible outcomes enumerated, four categories, n = 2,110; every other method and every variant we tried lands between 10−30 and 10−36)
  • Taken one list at a time, the chance of a random sample putting Studentska lista at or below 40.0% when its true share was 53.0% is 2 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 4 followed by 32 zeros); the chance of putting Ujedinjena Srbija at or above 47.4% when its true share was 39.0% is 2 × 10−15 (about 1 in a 4 followed by 14 zeros).
  • Asking for both at once (Studentska lista at or below 40.0% and Ujedinjena Srbija at or above 47.4%) gives 2 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 4 followed by 32 zeros) exactly. The textbook chi-square approximation gives 3 × 10−36 (about 1 in a 3 followed by 35 zeros) with four categories and 1 × 10−33 (about 1 in a 9 followed by 32 zeros) with all lists kept separate.
  • Among two million simulated ideal random polls from the real electorate, none came close to Ipsos’s combination, under any of the definitions of “close” we tried.
  • The conclusion is unchanged for any sample size from 1,500 to 3,624, whether or not Kosovo i Metohija and the diaspora are removed from the population to match Ipsos’s sampling frame, and whether the comparison is made on all ballots or on valid votes only: the probability never rises above about 10−25.
  • By Ipsos’s own published margins of error, the true Studentska lista share lay 10.9 points outside the top of its 95% interval, 12 of its own standard errors from its estimate.
  • To make Ipsos’s result an ordinary 1-in-20 unlucky draw, about 450,000 voters would have had to move to Studentska lista in the three days between fieldwork and election day; even if every one of the 275,000 unexpected extra voters had voted Studentska, a further 298,000 would still have had to move. If a quarter of voters were undecided at the time of the poll, they would have had to vote 92% for Studentska lista, and even then the small-list excess remains unexplained.
# the headline exponent in words (short scale, as used in English; long scale, as used in Serbian)
pow_words <- function(l10) {
  # the number 1/p written as  lead × 10^e, then named: e.g. 3 × 10^36 = "three undecillion"
  e <- floor(-l10); lead <- round(10^(-l10 - e)); if (lead == 10) { lead <- 1; e <- e + 1 }
  grp <- e %/% 3; mult <- lead * 10^(e %% 3)                      # mult in 1..900
  short_names <- c(`10` = "nonillion", `11` = "decillion", `12` = "undecillion", `13` = "duodecillion")
  # Serbian forms: singular (1), paucal (2–4), plural (5+)
  long_names  <- list(`10` = c("kvintilion", "kvintiliona", "kvintiliona"), `11` = c("kvintilijarda", "kvintilijarde", "kvintilijardi"),
                      `12` = c("sekstilion", "sekstiliona", "sekstiliona"), `13` = c("sekstilijarda", "sekstilijarde", "sekstilijardi"))
  if (!as.character(grp) %in% names(short_names)) return(sprintf("one in a %d followed by %d zeros", lead, e))
  en_small <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine")
  en_tens  <- c("ten", "twenty", "thirty", "forty", "fifty", "sixty", "seventy", "eighty", "ninety")
  en_mult  <- if (mult < 10) en_small[mult] else if (mult < 100) en_tens[mult / 10] else paste(en_small[mult / 100], "hundred")
  sr_small <- c("", "dva", "tri", "četiri", "pet", "šest", "sedam", "osam", "devet")
  sr_tens  <- c("deset", "dvadeset", "trideset", "četrdeset", "pedeset", "šezdeset", "sedamdeset", "osamdeset", "devedeset")
  sr_hund  <- c("sto", "dvesta", "trista", "četiristo", "petsto", "šeststo", "sedamsto", "osamsto", "devetsto")
  sr_mult  <- if (mult < 10) sr_small[mult] else if (mult < 100) sr_tens[mult / 10] else sr_hund[mult / 100]
  sr_form  <- if (mult == 1) 1 else if (mult %% 10 %in% 2:4 && !(mult %% 100 %in% 12:14)) 2 else 3
  sr_name  <- long_names[[as.character(grp)]][sr_form]
  sprintf("**one in %s %s** (a %d followed by %d zeros; in the long-scale naming used in Serbian and most of continental Europe, *%s*)",
          en_mult, short_names[as.character(grp)], lead, e, trimws(paste(sr_mult, sr_name)))
}

10.3 What it means, and what it does not

Sampling error alone cannot account for the gap. The hypothesis that Ipsos’s published numbers are what a random sample of actual voters would produce, with chance as the only source of discrepancy, is rejected by every method: the exact probability is about 2 × 10−36, that is, roughly one in five hundred decillion (a 5 followed by 35 zeros; in the long-scale naming used in Serbian and most of continental Europe, petsto kvintilijardi). Depending on the definition of “at least as far from the truth”, on the test used and on the treatment of invalid ballots, the figure moves between 10−30 and 10−36; at this depth a few powers of ten change nothing. For a sense of scale: picking one specific star at random from all the roughly 1024 stars in the observable universe is a 1-in-1024 event, and that is about 1012 times more likely than Ipsos’s result under random sampling. No reasonable choice of sample size, population definition, base or test statistic changes that conclusion. Ipsos’s own stated precision leads to the same conclusion without any modelling on our part.

What the numbers do not establish on their own is the cause. Several candidate explanations remain, and statistics alone cannot pick between them, nor rule out a combination; the evidence in this document bears on each as follows:

  • A genuine late swing. Possible in principle, and flagged by Ipsos itself as a caveat; but it would have had to involve some 450,000 voters moving to the student list within 72 hours, among them roughly one in 7 of all Ujedinjena Srbija supporters, a movement several times larger than the late swings documented in comparable elections, and one that no other evidence from those three days suggests.
  • Differential turnout. Ruled out as a sufficient explanation in its net form: even the most extreme assumption about the unexpected extra voters leaves the gap essentially intact. Gross flows (intending voters staying home while others turned out) cannot be assessed from outside; they belong under non-sampling error below.
  • Undecided voters. A quarter of the electorate undecided and then voting 92% for one list would reconcile the two big numbers; nothing reconciles the small-list excess. A real but modest contribution is plausible; a full explanation is not.
  • Non-sampling error (telephone coverage, non-response, concealment of intention, mode and house effects, likely-voter modelling, weighting; see total survey error). This is the explanation that the test cannot address directly, and every poll carries some of it. What the test does establish is its required size: a non-sampling bias large enough to explain Ipsos’s numbers would have to move the two large lists by 13 and 8 points, a margin error of about 21 points. A catalogue of 37 documented poll misses from 2010 to 2026 ranks that fifth-largest overall and third among elections. The larger misses are two referendums (Colombia 2016, Greece 2015) and two polls of the Costa Rican run-off of 2018 published 11 to 16 days before the vote. Among election polls with final-week fieldwork, samples of two thousand or more, a disclosed commissioning party and an undisputed count, it has no counterpart in that catalogue. Ipsos’s election-night projection with CeSID was accurate to within a few tenths of a point, but that projection rested on counted ballots at sampled polling stations, not on interviews, so it does not share the pre-election survey’s sources of error and does not by itself tell us how large those could have been.
  • Misrepresentation of the published numbers. The data are consistent with it, exactly as they are consistent with a sufficiently large version of each explanation above; the test cannot separate them. The fact that the poll was commissioned by one of the contestants is a reason to ask for transparency, not evidence of intent, and this document makes no claim about intent.

The defensible public statement is therefore: Ipsos’s final pre-election numbers cannot have arisen from random sampling error. What remains is some combination of a late swing far larger than any for which there is independent evidence, a turnout or undecided-voter shift of a size documented only in a few referendums and one run-off polled more than a week out, a methodological bias far larger than final pre-election polls ordinarily carry, and the published numbers not reflecting what the survey measured. This document cannot distinguish among these, nor between any of them and misreporting. Doing so requires what a probability calculation cannot supply: Ipsos’s raw data, its weighting scheme, its likely-voter model, and its treatment of undecided respondents.

10.4 Caveats

  • RIK’s results used here are preliminary (8,339 of 8,392 polling stations, snapshot of 31 October 2026, 11:00 CET), and they are taken as the truth throughout. The outstanding 0.6% of polling stations cannot move the national shares by more than a few tenths of a point. Re-knitting this document with the final figures entered in Section 3 will update every computed number automatically.
  • The effective sample size is inferred from Ipsos’s published intervals, not stated by Ipsos. The sensitivity analysis shows the conclusion is insensitive to it. The counts “out of 2,110” are a construction that matches the precision of Ipsos’s intervals, not interviews Ipsos actually conducted.
  • The headline figure is computed exactly, by enumeration, and carries no simulation error. The chi-square figures are asymptotic approximations and are read as orders of magnitude; Pearson’s chi-square is reported for completeness but is known to be unreliable this far into the tail. The importance-sampling estimate is reported only to document that, with a proposal centred on Ipsos’s numbers, it undercounts the tail by a factor of about 6 (its runs spread over 0.9 in the exponent, which understates its true error).
  • Ipsos’s percentages are published to one decimal place; converting them to counts introduces errors of up to about one respondent per category, which is immaterial in Scheme A but a reason to treat the smallest Scheme B cells as indicative only.
  • Ipsos’s assumed 2.5% invalid share is not a sampled quantity; Section 8 shows the effect of removing it from the comparison (a few powers of ten, conclusion unchanged).
  • Minority lists are defined here as the four that won seats. Other lists representing national minorities (e.g. Zukorlić (SPP)) are in the “Other” category in both sources, so the comparison is consistent.

11.2 References

For every statistical and methodological concept used above, one or two sound, readable resources and the corresponding Wikipedia article. All links were checked on 31 October 2026.

Probability distributions

  • Multinomial distribution. Blitzstein, J. K. & Hwang, J. (2019). Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., ch. 7 “Joint distributions”. Free online at probabilitybook.net · Weisstein, E. W., Multinomial Distribution, Wolfram MathWorld (formulas incl. covariance) · Wikipedia.
  • Binomial distribution and its normal approximation. Seeing Theory, ch. 3 “Probability Distributions”, Brown University (interactive) · Wikipedia.
  • Multinomial cumulative probabilities (the pmultinom algorithm). Levin, B. (1981). A representation for multinomial cumulative distribution functions. Annals of Statistics 9(5), 1123–1126. doi:10.1214/aos/1176345593 · Davis, A. pmultinom: One-Sided Multinomial Probabilities, R package, CRAN.

Sampling error, confidence intervals, sample size

  • Standard error and confidence interval for a proportion. Seeing Theory, ch. 4 “Frequentist Inference” (interactive) · Wikipedia: Binomial proportion confidence interval.
  • Margin of error in polls. Pew Research Center (2016), Understanding the margin of error in election polls · Wikipedia.
  • Design effect and effective sample size. Zipf, G. & Valliant, R., Design Effects and Effective Sample Size, PracTools vignette (CRAN) · Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. Wiley (the original source of the weighting design-effect formula) · Wikipedia.
  • z-scores and “sigma” levels. Wikipedia: Standard score · Wikipedia: 68–95–99.7 rule.

Hypothesis testing

  • p-values and tail probabilities. Wasserstein, R. L. & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician 70(2), 129–133. doi:10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108 (free access) · Wikipedia.
  • Goodness-of-fit tests (Pearson chi-square, G / likelihood-ratio) and the chi-square distribution. McDonald, J. H. (2014). Handbook of Biological Statistics, 3rd ed.: Chi-square test of goodness-of-fit, G-test of goodness-of-fit, Small numbers in chi-square and G-tests · Wikipedia: Goodness of fit, Pearson’s chi-squared test, G-test, Likelihood-ratio test, Chi-squared distribution.
  • Exact tests and Monte Carlo (simulation-based) p-values. Downey, A. (2011), There is only one test! · VanderPlas, J. (2016), Statistics for Hackers, PyCon (video) · Wikipedia: Exact test, Monte Carlo method.
  • Importance sampling (estimating very small probabilities by simulation). Owen, A. B. (2013), Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples, ch. 9 “Importance sampling”, free online at artowen.su.domains/mc · Wikipedia.
  • Asymptotic (large-sample) approximations and their limits in the far tail. Wikipedia: Asymptotic distribution · the G statistic’s exact tail behaviour follows from Sanov’s theorem (Wikipedia).
  • Why probabilities are computed in logarithms. Wikipedia: Arithmetic underflow.

Polling methodology

  • Sampling vs non-sampling error. Groves, R. M. & Lyberg, L. (2010). Total survey error: past, present, and future. Public Opinion Quarterly 74(5), 849–879 · Wikipedia: Total survey error.
  • How large polling errors normally are; late swings. Jennings, W. & Wlezien, C. (2018). Election polling errors across time and space. Nature Human Behaviour 2, 276–283. doi:10.1038/s41562-018-0315-6 (30,000+ polls, 351 elections, 45 countries).
  • Diagnosing a polling miss (non-response, turnout models, “shy” voters). AAPOR Task Force (2021), 2020 Pre-Election Polling: An Evaluation of the 2020 General Election Polls.
  • Turnout and likely-voter models. Keeter, S. & Igielnik, R. (2016), Can Likely U.S. Voter Models Be Improved?, Pew Research Center.
